input: This memo considers the case for fitting vibration and temperature sensors across the pump population in order to reduce unplanned downtime. The plant operates 180 pumps, and the maintenance records for the past 12 months show a total of 1035 h of unplanned downtime, which represents a significant burden on production. Bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours, making them the largest single contributor and a natural focus for any monitoring programme. The downtime is spread across the year rather than concentrated in a single incident, and it recurs in a pattern that planned intervention could in principle interrupt, which is what makes monitoring a plausible response to it. A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $456k installed, with a further $73k per year in ongoing costs. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 24%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so its transferability remains uncertain. A more cautious first step is also available: a pilot on 21 pumps would cost $43k over three months. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. On balance, this memo recommends proceeding with the three-month pilot in the first instance; the reliability engineering group would own the pilot and report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation would be held until the pilot results have been reported and considered in full.
target: Run the three-month pilot before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. The evidence base is the plant's maintenance records for 12 months across 180 pumps. The records show 1035 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. Bearings are the failure the sensors address: a sensor set detects the vibration and temperature rise that precede a bearing failure, in time to plan the repair inside a scheduled stop rather than lose the pump in service. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $456k installed, plus $73k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit the sensors cut downtime by 24%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. The pilot covers 21 pumps and costs $43k over three months. It measures the downtime reduction on this plant's pumps, under this plant's operating pattern, which is the figure the full-installation decision needs and the vendor trial cannot give. The pilot also tests the detection chain in service: whether the sensors raise alarms the maintenance crew can act on, whether the alarms arrive early enough to plan around, and whether false alarms stay rare enough to keep the alarms credible. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: detection shortens the response, not the supply chain, and a detected failure still waits for its part. The decision the pilot informs is whether the measured reduction justifies the full installation cost, and that decision stands at the March capital review with the pilot results in front of it.
